doc.title: Karl Berger interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, August 11, 2014

title: Avoiding the word jazz; pulse, Bach and tempered tuning
summary: Berger avoids the word jazz, argues European music turned to form, that Bach improvised, and that tempered tuning is artificial, tying it to Ornette.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Did you avoid the word jazz?

Yeah, yeah. As much as possible. Because you know if I mention the word jazz in a room with 20 people, each of these 20 people have a completely different sound in their head. So this word is no longer functional. It really isn’t. It is functional in the sense that there is a sense of propulsion that you have in world music, which sort of got lost in European music. European music got much more into form and more and more into form, and is being thought of and listened to from the form element and not from the propulsion of the music, which is like in every world music area, whether you go to Africa to the Mid-East where you go, wherever you go you’re going to hear a beat. Right? It’s mostly played by drums. But even if it’s not played by drums you’re going to play from a beat. And classical music until the nineteenth century was played that way too. There was no conductors in Bach’s time or even Mozart’s time. There were not real conductors.
The music had a pulse which kept everybody together.

Yeah. You played from a pulse or you played like jazz. And as a matter of fact I think that Bach’s music — I don’t think that Bach ever played the piano, the organ charts or the keyboard charts that he wrote for himself. You know when you look at his scores there’s no corrections, he’s improvising. There’s no corrections in the scores when you look at his manuscripts. So that means he was just improvising. So I imagine he wasn’t looking at the score when he played on Sunday morning, he just played. © Fillius Jazz Archive -7-

Yeah. So basically that whole idea of jazz is nothing new you know. And I would also imagine from the international point of view, Baroque music probably sounded a lot more like Moroccan music or something. Because the idea of tempered tuning was just invented then.

Or any non-tempered music. Because the tempered system was invented at the same time. So the people who played at that time were not really accustomed to hear it this way. You know? That was just for the composer to be able to manipulate the changes, but the players were still non-tempered players. So it must have been a completely different sound than what we are hearing now. Now it sounds very artificial actually.
The tuning. The classical tuning is very artificial from a point of world musical viewpoint — of a non-tempered intonation.
Wasn’t that part of Ornette Coleman’s approach about this note can be played here or it can be played here, depending on how I feel.
Doesn’t he say that about my voice, right? It can be translated into many languages.

Yeah. Right. Yeah, exactly. That’s exactly it. Like Ornette is very aware of that and has done — like his whole harmolodic thing is about that. So yeah. What we are hearing now is sort of a distilled version of tempered tuning, which is like an artificial system.
